subject: Environment
sub_topic: Air Prevention and Control of Pollution Act 1981

concepts.name: Legislative Background and Constitutional Basis
key_dimensions: Enacted under Article 253 read with Entry 13 of Union List (international treaties) following Stockholm Conference 1972
Concurrent List Entry 17A (forests) vs actual placement — understanding why environment legislation uses Article 253
Relationship with 42nd Constitutional Amendment 1976 inserting Article 48A and Article 51A(g)
Distinction from Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974 in terms of legislative trigger

concepts.name: Definition of 'Air Pollutant' and 'Air Pollution' under the Act
key_dimensions: Statutory definition under Section 2(a) — any solid, liquid, or gaseous substance in concentrations injurious to human beings, living creatures, plants, or property
Inclusion of noise as an air pollutant via 1987 Amendment — a frequent UPSC trap
Comparison with definition under Environment Protection Act 1986 — overlap and distinction
Implication of the word 'prescribed' — delegated legislative power to include new substances

concepts.name: Definition and Scope of 'Industry' and 'Industrial Plant'
key_dimensions: Section 2(k) definition — any industry, operation, or process which emits air pollutants
Whether agriculture-related burning activities fall under 'industrial plant' — grey area
UPSC trap: difference between 'industry' under this Act vs 'industry' under Water Act 1974
Role of State Boards in expanding or restricting the list of industries requiring consent

concepts.name: Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) — Constitution and Functions
key_dimensions: Constituted under Section 3 — but note it was originally constituted under Water Act 1974 and its powers were extended to Air Act (Section 3 simply extends CPCB, does not create a new body)
Composition: Chairman appointed by Central Government, members from ministries, experts — distinction from State Board composition
Functions under Section 16 — advisory role to Central Government vs executive role of State Boards
Power to lay down standards for quality of air (ambient air quality standards) — Section 16(h)

concepts.name: State Pollution Control Board (SPCB) — Constitution, Powers, and Conflict with CPCB
key_dimensions: Section 4 — State Government constitutes SPCB; where a Board exists under Water Act, same Board functions under Air Act
Section 18 — State Boards subject to directions of Central Government (not just CPCB) — a key hierarchy trap
Distinction: CPCB coordinates and supervises; SPCB implements on ground — exam often tests who 'grants consent'
Conflict resolution mechanism — Section 18(2) Central Government direction overrides State Board decisions

concepts.name: Consent Mechanism — Section 21 (Prohibition without Consent)
key_dimensions: No person can establish or operate any industrial plant in an air pollution control area without prior consent of SPCB — Section 21
Deemed consent provision — if SPCB does not respond within 4 months, consent is deemed granted (trap: compare with Water Act's similar provision)
Conditions attached to consent — SPCB can impose technology, emission, and operational conditions
Distinction between 'establishment' consent and 'operation' consent — both required separately

concepts.name: Air Pollution Control Areas — Declaration and Significance
key_dimensions: Section 19 — State Government may declare any area as air pollution control area AFTER consultation with SPCB (not unilaterally)
Entire state can be declared as one air pollution control area — important for coverage
Trap: Central Government has NO direct power to declare air pollution control areas — it is exclusively a State Government power
Consequence of declaration — Section 21 consent requirement is triggered only within such areas

concepts.name: Powers of Entry, Inspection, and Sampling — Sections 24–26
key_dimensions: Section 24 — SPCB officers empowered to enter, inspect premises, examine registers, take samples
Section 25 — Procedure for taking air samples — two-container method similar to Water Act (trap: exact procedure differs slightly between Acts)
Section 26 — Analysis of samples by Government Analyst; certificate admissible as evidence
Limitation: Entry powers cannot be exercised without reasonable grounds — protection against arbitrary action

concepts.name: Power to Give Directions — Section 31A and Closure/Restraint Orders
key_dimensions: Section 31A — Central Government can issue directions to any person/authority including closure, prohibition, or regulation of any industry
This power was inserted by 1987 Amendment — making it concurrent with EPA 1986 Section 5 directions
UPSC trap: Under original 1981 Act, there was no Section 31A — it came via amendment; compare with EPA 1986 which had this from inception
Directions under Section 31A vs directions under Section 18 — Section 18 is for State Boards, Section 31A is for industries/persons

concepts.name: 1987 Amendment — Key Changes and Significance
key_dimensions: Inclusion of noise as an air pollutant — most tested amendment provision
Insertion of Section 31A — power to issue directions including closure orders
Enhancement of penalties — increased stringency for violations
Alignment with Environment Protection Act 1986 — post-Bhopal disaster legislative tightening; 1987 amendment brought Air Act closer to EPA framework

concepts.name: Offences, Penalties, and Cognizance of Offences — Sections 37–42
key_dimensions: Section 37 — Failure to comply with provisions: imprisonment minimum 1.5 years extendable to 6 years PLUS fine (trap: minimum imprisonment is mandatory)
Section 40 — Offences by companies: every person in charge at time of offence is liable (doctrine of vicarious liability for directors)
Section 41 — Offences by Government departments: Head of Department is deemed guilty
Section 43 — No court shall take cognizance of offence except on complaint by Board or officer authorized — bars private criminal complaints (compare: EPA 1986 Section 19 has similar bar)

concepts.name: Citizen's Right to Approach Court — Section 42 and Judicial Remedies
key_dimensions: Section 42 — Any person can make complaint to court if Board fails to act after 60 days notice to Board (saves citizen from total dependence on Board)
Comparison with Water Act 1974 Section 49 — identical structure, same 60-day notice period
Judicial interpretation: NGT and High Courts have used this provision to expand standing
Limitation: Complaint must be preceded by 60-day notice to Board — courts have held this as mandatory, not directory

concepts.name: Relationship between Air Act 1981 and Environment Protection Act 1986
key_dimensions: EPA 1986 is an umbrella legislation; Air Act 1981 is a specific legislation — lex specialis principle
Section 24 of EPA — provisions of EPA shall be in addition to, and not in derogation of, Air Act and Water Act
Overlap in emission standards — CPCB standards under Air Act vs MoEFCC notifications under EPA
Trap: EPA 1986 confers broader powers on Central Government directly; Air Act routes power through CPCB-SPCB hierarchy

concepts.name: Standards for Emission and Ambient Air Quality — Section 16 and 17
key_dimensions: Section 16(h) — CPCB lays down standards for quality of air (ambient air quality standards) — advisory/recommendatory for States

Section 17(1)(g) — SPCB lays down standards for emission from industrial plants within State — must not be less stringent than CPCB standards (trap: States can only make standards MORE stringent, not less)
National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) notified by CPCB — legal status under this section
Difference between emission standards (from source) and ambient air quality standards (in environment) — often confused in questions

concepts.name: Automobile Emissions and Applicability of the Act
key_dimensions: Original 1981 Act did not cover vehicular emissions — major lacuna
Section 20 — after declaration of air pollution control area, State Government may restrict use of certain fuels or appliances (indirect vehicle control)
Vehicular emissions primarily regulated through Motor Vehicles Act 1988 and EPA 1986 notifications (Bharat Stage norms) — Air Act's limited direct role
Supreme Court's role in filling gap: MC Mehta v Union of India (CNG mandate for Delhi) used EPA 1986 and constitutional provisions, not Air Act directly

concepts.name: Power to Obtain Information and Access to Data — Section 24 and Section 31
key_dimensions: Section 31 — Boards can establish air quality monitoring stations and laboratories
Section 24 — Right to inspect registers, records, and take samples — creates transparency obligation on industries
Boards can require industries to install continuous emission monitoring systems (CEMS) — regulatory evolution beyond Act's text
Trap: Board's own monitoring data is primary; industry self-reported data is secondary — Board is not bound by industry submissions

concepts.name: Appeals Mechanism — Section 31 (Appellate Authority)
key_dimensions: Section 31 — Any person aggrieved by SPCB's order on consent (grant, refusal, conditions) may appeal to Appellate Authority within 30 days
Appellate Authority constituted by State Government — not a court, quasi-judicial body
Trap: Appeal lies against SPCB orders, NOT against Central Government or CPCB directions under Section 18 or 31A
After National Green Tribunal Act 2010 — appeals from Appellate Authority decisions can go to NGT (jurisdictional overlap question)

concepts.name: National Green Tribunal (NGT) and Air Act — Interface and Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: Schedule I of NGT Act 2010 includes Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981 — NGT has jurisdiction over disputes under this Act
NGT can hear appeals against orders/decisions of authorities under Air Act — replaced some High Court jurisdiction
Trap: NGT cannot hear cases under Air Act where 'substantial question relating to environment' is not involved
MC Mehta cases — pre-NGT Supreme Court jurisprudence on air pollution now supplemented by NGT orders; both remain valid precedents

concepts.name: Comparison: Air Act 1981 vs Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974
key_dimensions: Water Act 1974 was the first pollution control legislation in India; Air Act 1981 modelled on it — same institutional framework (CPCB/SPCB)
Key structural difference: Water Act created CPCB; Air Act merely extended CPCB's powers — CPCB is a single body serving both Acts
Consent mechanism: Both require prior consent but Air Act's 'air pollution control area' declaration is a precondition (no such geographic precondition in Water Act)
Penalty comparison: Air Act 1981 has higher minimum imprisonment than original Water Act 1974 — reflects post-industrial awareness

concepts.name: Judicial Interpretations — Landmark Cases under Air Act
key_dimensions: MC Mehta v Union of India (1987) — Absolute liability principle for hazardous industries; expanded reading of air pollution liability beyond Act's text
MC Mehta v Union of India (Taj Trapezium Case, 1996) — Supreme Court used Air Act + EPA to restrict polluting industries near Taj Mahal; relocation orders
Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v Union of India (1996) — Precautionary principle and polluter pays principle read into Air Act and EPA as part of customary international law
Trap: Many landmark 'environment' cases cite Air Act alongside EPA 1986 and Article 21 — UPSC questions often ask which specific Act was the primary basis
